partyRegisteredTitle: This application is in the registry (ou=applications).
partyUnregisteredTitle: No entry under ou=applications names this. The registry holds what this service has been ASKED ABOUT — a client_id presented, an AppliesTo a token was issued for, an SPN a ticket was cut for — and this delegation named something nobody has otherwise mentioned. That is ordinary for an RFC 8693 audience and is worth seeing rather than hiding.
partyNoneTitle: Nothing here names this party, and on some mechanisms nothing can: a forwarded ticket-granting ticket is handed to whichever service the client chooses, and this KDC is never told which.
modeImpersonationTitle: What came out names the initial identity and nothing else. The far end cannot tell an intermediary was involved, and neither can anybody reading the credential afterwards — which is why the issuer is the only place this is ever visible.
modeDelegationTitle: What came out CARRIES the chain: an `act` claim, a composite ActAs, or S4U_DELEGATION_INFO in the PAC. The far end can see who is really asking.
s4u2selfNote: [MS-SFU] protocol transition: impersonation, whatever follows it
s4u2proxyNote: [MS-SFU] constrained delegation: always delegation, even after S4U2Self — the ticket carries the chain in S4U_DELEGATION_INFO
outcomeRefusedTitle: This service refused the delegation. The reason is the KDC's own words — the same text the client was sent — rather than a second wording written for this page.
rowChainTitle: Draw THIS relationship on its own — the whole chain this act belongs to, with everything else in the service left out.
nodeIdentifierTitle: What a protocol would have to present to reach this party, and that protocol's own word for it. It is the second line inside the box in the picture above; where the label IS the identifier, only the word is drawn.
shapeDashedTitle: Neither ou=users nor ou=applications holds an entry for this. The shape is the one its role implies.
shapeDashed: drawn from its role — neither store knows it
selfTargetTitle: S4U2Self is a request for a ticket to yourself, so the intermediary and the target are one party. There is no line for it in the picture because an arrow leaving a box and coming back is a drawing of nothing.
thisPageTitle: This is the person this page is about. Every line on the picture starts or ends here.
notInDelegationTitle: This box is in no delegation at all — it holds credentials from an ordinary grant. The delegation roles are a fact about the OTHER register.
noHolderTitle: Nothing holds this one. An X509-SVID has no audience, and a token can be minted with no client_id — this service issued it and there is no second party to draw.
noIdentifierTitle: A Kerberos ticket has no identifier this service could quote — there is no jti and no AssertionID in one.
noSessionTitle: No browser sign-on session was stated. That is true of every direct grant — client_credentials, password, the pre-authorized code, a token exchange — and of everything issued outside the token endpoint.
oidcNameTitle: OpenID Connect's name for the same exchange. One thing, two vocabularies.
notOauthGrantTitle: A SAML assertion, a Kerberos ticket and an SVID are issued by protocols that have never heard of an OAuth grant. The mechanism named here is their own specification's.
flowNotStated: Whatever minted this said nothing about how. That is true of every JWT signed outside the token endpoint — WS-Trust's JWT token type and the credential issuer both sign directly — and of the signed UserInfo response, which is a reply rather than a credential a grant produced.
issuedToAskedTitle: This service handed that party a credential. It goes to whoever ASKED.
issuedToTitle: This service handed that party a credential.
jumpsTitleForwarded: Nobody named this party on these acts, so the line jumps it. A forwarded ticket-granting ticket has no intermediary and cannot have one.
jumpsTitle: Nobody named this party on these acts, so the line jumps it.
nothingDecides: Nothing in this service decides who may perform this act.
noActorTitle: A forwarded ticket-granting ticket has no intermediary this KDC was told about.
appChooserEmpty: No delegation held here names an application yet, so there is nothing to choose between. An application arrives in this list the moment something delegates through it or to it: an RFC 8693 audience or the client_id that performed the exchange, a WS-Trust AppliesTo, or the service principal a Kerberos S4U request asked for a ticket to.
appChooserPlaceholder: part of a client_id, an SPN or an audience
appChooserNothing: No application any act named matches that. This list holds what some delegation actually presented, spellings and all, so a name that is in the acts table above and not in here is one this register filed as a person rather than as an application.
userChooserEmpty: Nothing has authenticated here and no delegation names anybody, so there is nobody to choose. An identity arrives in this list the moment a credential is accepted in any of the sixteen families, the moment a token or an assertion is issued naming somebody, or the moment a delegation names them — including one they were never present for.
userChooserPlaceholder: part of a username, a principal or a subject
userChooserNothing: Nobody here matches that. This list is the identity register UNIONED with everybody a delegation named, so a name that is on the page above and not in here reached this service as an application rather than as a person.
defaultPermissionsTitle: The token names this resource and none of its delegated permissions — which is what a scope naming the resource's client_id produces, because that value becomes the audience and comes off the scope claim. It is also what a resource that defines no permissions can ever produce.
noModeTitle: Impersonation and delegation are properties of a DELEGATION mechanism. An ordinary grant makes neither claim, and calling it one would be this console inventing a judgement.
appNotRegisteredTitle: No entry under ou=applications names this. The registry holds what this service has been ASKED ABOUT; a delegation can name something nobody has otherwise mentioned.
noAppNamed: No delegation held here names an application.
authenticatedHereTitle: A credential was accepted for this name here, so the identity register has a row for them.
namedInDelegationTitle: Some delegation act names them, in one of the three roles. That does NOT mean they were present — S4U2Self and OnBehalfOf name somebody who proved nothing.
neverAuthenticatedTitle: Nothing has ever presented a credential under this name in this process. Something was issued in it, or somebody delegated using it, which is exactly the state worth noticing.
clientNotPersonTitle: Something authenticated as this name and said it was a client rather than a person — the client_credentials grant is the usual way.
nobodyAuthenticated: Nobody has authenticated here and no delegation names anybody.
allowedEmptyBefore: No application in this registry exposes an API or holds a permission yet, so there is nothing to search. An application arrives in this list the moment it is given a base URI or a permission of its own — which makes it a RESOURCE — or is granted one somebody else exposes, which makes it a CLIENT. Both are done on
baseUriOnly: a base URI and nothing on it yet
groupOwn: in no group but its own
groupOneOf: one of {n} applications joined to each other
allowedPlaceholder: part of a client_id, a base URI or an application name
allowedNothingBefore: No application in the configured register matches that. This list holds what the PERMISSION register touches — an entry with a base URI or a permission of its own, or one holding a grant — so a name that is on
allowedNothingAfter: and not in here is an application nothing has been configured about yet.
ldapmodifyOnlyTitle: No entry under ou=applications answers to this identifier. It can only have got here through an ldapmodify, since both console doors read the registry.
namedForTitle: A group is named after the application whose identifier sorts first, so that adding a grant inside it does not rename it.
noLinesTitle: Nothing in this group may reach anything else in it. A group of one with a base URI is an API somebody described and nothing was granted on.
unusedTitle: Granted and never requested. Read off the client's own oauthScope — evidence rather than proof.
danglingCountTitle: Naming a permission no application in this registry defines. Not drawn on any picture, because a line to nowhere would be a drawing of a resource that is there.
selfGrantsTitle: An application granted its own permission. Neither console door will create one; an ldapmodify can. No arrow is drawn, because an arrow from a box back to itself is a drawing of nothing.
noGroups: Nothing in this registry exposes an API or holds a permission, so there are no groups to draw.
noPermissionIdTitle: This permission has no identifier because its application has no oauthPermissionBaseUri. A permission is named by its base URI followed by its name, so no client can ever ask for this one. Set the base on the application and it resolves.
noPermissionId: no identifier — the application has no base URI
nobodyHoldsTitle: Nothing holds this permission. That is the ordinary state of a permission that has just been defined — defining one grants it to nobody.
changeRemoveTitle: This page draws the register and does not change it. The Remove button for this permission is on Protocols › Delegation.
danglingTitle: No application in this registry defines this permission. Either the resource's entry was deleted, or the permission was removed from it while this grant still named it, or an ldapmodify wrote a grant that never resolved — both console doors refuse to create one.
doesNotResolve: nothing — the permission does not resolve, so this scope is treated as an ordinary one
askedTitle: This client's entry records having asked for this scope. It is evidence rather than proof: oauthScope records what was requested, not what was issued.
neverAskedTitle: This client has never asked for it. A configured grant nobody has needed is exactly what this register is here to show.
changeRevokeTitle: This page draws the register and does not change it. The Revoke button for this grant is on Protocols › Delegation.
hPolicy: Who may act for whom — WS-Trust, token exchange and Kerberos
policyLead: Decided by the issuance policy (#186), from facts on the entries — one set of settings for the three protocols. appAllowedToDelegateTo on an application names the applications it delegates to (the analogue of msDS-AllowedToDelegateTo); appAllowedToActOnBehalfOf on the TARGET names the actors it accepts (the resource-based one); appDelegationSubjectGroup narrows who an actor may act for; and appDelegationSemantics says whether it may IMPERSONATE as well as delegate (empty is delegation only), with appDefaultDelegationSemantics the default. A person acting needs the role delegation.actorRole names. A person carrying stsNotDelegated, an application carrying appNotDelegated, or a member of
policyNeverDelegated: , is never delegated. The rules are the issuance policy's (action-ids choose-exchange-semantics and exchange-token); a realm changes them in its own policy.
policyEnforced: This realm is in product mode, so this is ENFORCED: a refusal is wst:RequestFailed, invalid_request or invalid_target.
policyNotEnforced: This realm is in development mode, so nothing is refused: the policy is asked and each act above says what WOULD have been refused in product.
policyEdit: Edit an application's on its own page, and a person's on theirs. GET /admin-api/delegation/policy is this section as JSON.
noPairsEnforced: No application here names a delegation target or an intermediary it accepts, so every WS-Trust and token-exchange delegation is refused.
noPairsDevelopment: No application here names a delegation target or an intermediary it accepts, so every WS-Trust and token-exchange delegation is one product would refuse.
noIntermediaries: No application carries delegation semantics, appNotDelegated or a subject group.
mayActNote: stsMayAct is a person's own choice of the one party who may act for them; the access tokens issued about them carry it as RFC 8693's may_act, and a token exchange of one by anybody else is refused in every mode.
hAllowed: What is ALLOWED, decided in advance
allowedEvidence: Everything above this heading is EVIDENCE and everything below it is INTENT, and the difference is the most useful thing on this page. The acts, the chains and the picture they are drawn from are things that happened — a credential was issued or refused, at a moment, to somebody. What follows is CONFIGURATION: which client applications may reach which resource applications, typed in before anybody asked for anything. Read one against the other and two questions answer themselves: which grants has nobody ever used, and what has been delegated that nobody granted.
allowedResourceBefore: A RESOURCE application exposes an API and a CLIENT application is granted permissions on it. The resource is given a base URI — anything absolute works here — and a list of permissions. A permission is identified by the two joined together — base https://example.com/ and name write make https://example.com/write — and a client application is granted some of them. A permission must be DEFINED before it can be GRANTED, which is the one ordering rule this feature has; it is checked in applications.js so that this form, the management API and the attribute editor on
allowedScope: Then a client asks for it as an OAuth scope, and the access token says both halves. scope=openid https://example.com/write produces a token audienced to https://example.com/ carrying scope: openid write — the base becomes the aud and the name becomes the scope, which is what a resource server wants: check the audience once, then read bare permission names. That is the same rule a scope naming another application's client_id already follows, one step more precise.
allowedProductBefore: In product mode an ungranted permission is refused invalid_scope, always. In development a grant refuses nothing by default, and that is a setting on
allowedProductAfter: With oauth2.delegatedPermissionsEnforced off — which it is unless somebody turned it on — an ungranted permission is honoured exactly as a granted one is, logged as ungranted, and marked here. With it on the same request is refused invalid_scope at the authorization endpoint, where the client can still be told. Both answers exercise a client and neither is the right one for every test, which is why the register is fully readable before anybody enforces anything.
seeAllowedPicture: See the allowed mappings as a picture
secondDiagramBefore: A SECOND diagram, and it is not the one above.
secondDiagramAfter: draws what happened: three layers, a stick figure for the person it happened to, and a hexagon for this service, which issued it. This one draws what is allowed: every box is an application, there is no person on it at all — a permission says webapp1 may reach the API as whoever is signed in, and there is no whoever yet — and this service is not on it either, because not one line of it has been issued. A line is DASHED until the client has actually asked for that permission, which is the reading a configured register exists for and the one an acts diagram can never give.
permissionsLead: One row per permission. Defining one grants it to nobody, so a row with nothing in the last two columns is the ordinary first step rather than a mistake. Removing a permission does NOT revoke the grants naming it — they stay on the clients' entries and become dangling, because tidying them would be this page writing to entries nobody named.
narrowPlaceholder: part of an application name or identifier
permSearchWhat: It matches the application that EXPOSES the permission — the first column — on its name and on its identifier both, and nothing else on the row. A permission belongs to exactly one application, so there is no second column this box could have meant. To find every permission some application HOLDS, search the grants table below instead: that is the relationship, and this table is the definition.
noPermMatch: No application whose name or identifier contains {wanted} exposes a permission.
permsElsewhere: {n} permission(s) are defined here under other applications.
noPermsAtAll: None is defined here at all yet.
noApiYet: No application here exposes an API yet. Give one a base URI below and then define a permission on it.
readOnlyBefore: This page READS the register and changes none of it (2026-10-01). Exposing an API, defining and removing a permission and revoking a grant are on
readOnlyMiddle: , for every application at once, and on each application's own Permissions tab under
readOnlyAfter: , for that one. Each row's last column links there instead of carrying a button.
exposeApiNote: The base URI is one answer per application and everything it exposes hangs off it. A trailing separator is added where there is none, because the identifier is a plain concatenation and https://example.com + write would otherwise read as one word. Clearing it leaves the permissions on the entry with no identifier at all, which the table above reports rather than hides.
definePermissionNote: The name is what ends up on the token's scope claim, so it must be a legal OAuth scope token: any printable ASCII except space, double quote and backslash (RFC 6749 section 3.3), and not |, which separates the name from the description in the attribute. The description is optional and is shown wherever the permission is; changing it means removing the permission and defining it again, because a permission has one description and two rows with one name would leave the second unreachable.
grantsLead: One row per (client, permission), and that IS the relationship. A client granted three permissions on one resource is three rows rather than one labelled 3, because the permission is what was granted and the pair of applications is what it happens to join. That is also how one-to-many and many-to-one both work here with no store of their own: three clients granted one permission is one value on each of three entries.
grantSearchWhat: It matches EITHER END of the relationship — the client that may ask and the resource that is reached — on the name and on the identifier both. Both ends deliberately, and it is the same argument the acts table's own text box makes: a reader arrives holding one application name and the question what is this thing mixed up in, and they do not know, and should not have to guess, which of the two columns it will turn up in. Searching one end would answer half that question while looking as though it had answered all of it. A DANGLING grant has no resource at all, so it matches only on its client — which is right: there is no other application in that row to find it by.
thTokenWillSay: What the access token will say
noGrantMatch: No grant names an application whose name or identifier contains {wanted}, at either end.
grantsElsewhere: {n} grant(s) are held here between other applications.
noGrantsAtAll: Nothing is granted here at all yet.
nothingGrantedYet: Nothing is granted yet. Define a permission above, then grant it on the client's own page — until then every scope this service is sent is an ordinary scope.
grantOnPagesBefore: This one is on the two applications' own pages. A grant lands on the CLIENT's entry, as a value of oauthDelegatedPermission, because the client is the party that will name the permission in a scope — so the entry that answers may this request be honoured is the entry the request identifies. Open an application under
grantOnPagesAfter: and its Permissions tab grants it somebody else's permission, or grants one of ITS OWN to another application — either way one half of the pair is settled by the page you are on rather than chosen out of a list of every application here. An application still cannot be granted its own permission: the token would be addressed to itself, which is what an ID Token already is, and neither page offers it.
nothingToGrantBefore: There is nothing to grant yet. A permission must be defined before it can be granted, so the control appears — on each application's own page under
nothingToGrantAfter: — once an application exposes one with an identifier. That ordering is the whole shape of the feature rather than a limitation of either page.
ordinaryAttributes: Every one of these is an ordinary attribute on an ordinary directory entry, and an ldapmodify reaches them exactly as it reaches a redirect URI: oauthPermissionBaseUri and oauthPermission on the resource, oauthDelegatedPermission on the client. What LDAP does not get is the ordering check — this directory enforces nothing anywhere — which is why a grant naming a permission nobody defines can exist at all, and why it is shown as dangling rather than treated as an error. GET /admin/ldap/applications publishes all three, and they persist wherever the directory does.
mapSameActsAfter: , with the time taken out and the parties shared.
mapMatched: It is drawn from everything that MATCHED the filter and not from one page of it. {n} act(s) match
mapAllInPicture: , and all of them are in the picture — paging a diagram would draw the boxes that happen to be on page 2 and the lines that happen to join them, which is a picture of the pagination.
textPlaceholder: a person, an SPN, a client_id, an attribute
mapSameFilter: The same filter the table has, so narrowing one narrows the other. Filtering to one person is how a busy picture is read — the text box searches every party of the chain and both explanations at once.
mapOnePartyInstead: Or draw one party's picture instead. These redraw around a single party rather than narrowing these acts: an application, with everything delegated through it or to it in either role — or a person, which is the wider picture of the two, because it adds every ordinary grant, assertion, ticket and SVID issued in their name and the sign-ins the lot rests on. None of that is a delegation, so none of it can be on this diagram.
mapNothing: Nothing has delegated anything yet, so there is nothing to draw.
mapNothingFiltered: Nothing has delegated anything yet that matches this filter, so there is nothing to draw.
mapNothingThree: Three things put a box on this page: a Kerberos S4U2Self, S4U2Proxy or forwarded-TGT request at the KDC; a WS-Trust RequestSecurityToken carrying <wst:OnBehalfOf> or <wst14:ActAs>; and an RFC 8693 token exchange at /oauth2/token. A REFUSED attempt counts and is drawn in red.
keyNote: The shapes are drawn by the same functions the picture uses, so a legend cannot come to describe a diagram this service no longer draws.
partiesNote: Every box, with both of its links where it has two. The picture can only put a shape inside ONE anchor, so a party that is a person AND an application links to the users page there and to both here.
noDirectory: No LDAP directory is loaded in this process, so nothing here can be resolved to a person and every box is drawn from its role. That is a build without ldap_server.js and not a failure.
relationshipsNote: Every line, as a sentence. The two kinds are different claims and the picture colours them differently: acts for is the DELEGATION relationship — who is acting on whose behalf — and reaches is the TRUST relationship, what the credential is FOR, which is the question what is this token's audience asked as a picture. The grey lines from the hexagon are neither: they are this service handing a credential to whoever asked for one.
lastColumnNote: The last column collapses one sentence and it is the same collapse the delegation table makes. Kerberos is the only family here that polices delegation at all, so a Kerberos row names an ATTRIBUTE and an account — short, and different on every row — while every WS-Trust and RFC 8693 row carries the identical paragraph saying that nothing checked it. Repeated down a table that paragraph is the column, so it is nothing checks this with the wording in the tooltip. A REFUSAL is never collapsed and prints in full: it is the KDC's own words, the same sentence the client was sent, and it is specific to the act rather than to the mechanism.
whatIssuedNote: Every credential that came out of an act in this picture, newest first — a Kerberos service ticket, a SAML assertion, an access token — with the chain it came out of. NO CREDENTIAL IS EVER HERE, only its kind and its identifier, which is the rule the audit log follows and which applies here for one more reason: a delegation act is precisely the request that carries two credentials at once. A Kerberos ticket genuinely has no identifier to quote, which this says rather than leaving a blank column to be read as a bug.
refusedProducedNothing: A REFUSED act produced nothing by definition, so it is not in this list — which is why {tokens} credential(s) sit under {acts} act(s) and the two numbers do not have to agree.
nothingIssuedThrough: Nothing has been issued through a delegation yet. A REFUSED act produces nothing, so a page of red lines and an empty table here is a consistent state rather than a broken one.
tokensLeftOff: {n} more credential(s) are not listed. This list holds at most {max} and keeps the newest; every one of them is still COUNTED on its line in the picture and in the relationship table, so what is lost is the individual identifiers of the oldest. Filter to narrow it.
impersonationInvisible: An IMPERSONATION is invisible everywhere else, and that is why the amber lines matter. Under a delegation the credential carries the chain, so a resource server can read the actor off the token afterwards. Under an impersonation nothing does: no reading of the token, at the far end or in a log, can recover the fact that a middle tier was involved. This diagram and the table behind it are the only places that fact will ever exist.
lineIsRelationship: A line is a RELATIONSHIP and not a request. Four acts a second apart between the same three parties are one line with 4 issued on it; the outcome is deliberately not part of a chain's identity, so a chain refused nine times and then fixed is one line that changes colour rather than two that never meet.
lineIsRelationshipAfter: is where the individual acts are, in order, with their times.
whoMayBefore: Who MAY delegate to whom is not on this page, because it is CONFIGURATION rather than history and it is Kerberos-only — Kerberos is the one family here that polices delegation at all. It is the second half of
whoMayAfter: , and the asymmetry between the two is worth reading there: the same picture, policed at one end and not at the other.
noScript: This page runs no script and neither does anything else in this console. The diagram is generated on the server and arrives as markup, which is why it does not pan, zoom or drag — and why nothing here relaxes script-src 'none'. Use the filter to narrow a busy picture, or take the document and open it in something that does zoom.
mapFormats: ?format=json carries the whole graph — the nodes, the edges, the credentials folded onto each edge, and the token list — and it is also in the graph member of GET /admin-api/delegation, so a test can assert what this page draws without parsing an SVG. ?format=svg is the document alone.
mapSameActsRest: A party that is the intermediary of six chains is ONE box here with six lines leaving it, which is the thing a table of rows cannot show and the reason to draw this at all. Every box and every line carries the whole story in its tooltip; the two tables under the picture say the same things in words, because a diagram nobody can quote is a diagram nobody can put in a bug report.
chainGone: No act held here belongs to that relationship. {key} names a chain this page can describe only while at least one of its acts is still held, and this store is CAPPED — it keeps at most {max} acts and drops the oldest first. So an old link coming back empty is the ordinary outcome rather than a mistake, and so is a link from a service that has restarted since: nothing here is persisted. Raise delegation.maxRecords on
chainGoneAfter: if this keeps happening to something you need.
chainNameOne: Name a relationship. This page draws ONE of them, and the way to it is a link on
chainNameOneAfter: — every row of both tables there has one, because the key that identifies a chain is (mechanism, initial identity, intermediary, target) and is not something worth typing.
wholePictureHeld: is everything that is still held, drawn together.
noIntermediaryNamed: with no intermediary this service was ever told the name of
happened: and it has happened {acts} time(s) — first {first}, last {last}.
chainIs: , with everything else in the service left out. A chain is (mechanism, initial identity, intermediary, target) and the OUTCOME is deliberately not part of it, so a relationship refused nine times and then fixed is this one page rather than two that never meet — which is why the acts below can be red and green at once.
chainIsAfter: is every relationship at once, where this one's parties are shared with the others they take part in.
chainParties: Up to three boxes — the layers of the architecture — with both of a party's links where it has two. A box here can carry more acts than this relationship has only if it played two roles in one of them, which is what S4U2Self is: the requester asks for a ticket to itself, so it is the intermediary AND the target.
chainRelationships: A chain has three parties and therefore up to TWO lines, and they are different claims: acts for is the DELEGATION relationship — who is acting on whose behalf — and reaches is the TRUST relationship, what the credential is FOR. The grey line from the hexagon is neither: it is this service handing a credential to whoever asked for one.
chainIssued: Every credential that came out of this relationship, newest first. NO CREDENTIAL IS EVER HERE, only its kind and its identifier — the rule the audit log follows, and one that applies here for one more reason: a delegation act is precisely the request that carries two credentials at once. A REFUSED act produced nothing by definition, which is why {tokens} credential(s) sit under {acts} act(s).
nothingIssuedOnChain: Nothing was issued on this relationship. A page of red acts and an empty table here is a consistent state rather than a broken one.
sameRowsAfter: holds, narrowed to this relationship and not paged — there are {n} of them and the cap on the whole store is {max}. This is where the TIMES are: the picture has them taken out, because four acts a second apart between the same three parties are one line.
chainFormats: ?format=json carries this chain, its acts and the graph behind the picture; ?format=svg is the document alone, with no links in it. There is no form on this page and therefore no operation on /admin-api — everything here is an observation, and the acts are in GET /admin-api/delegation where a caller can filter them.
appNoAct: No act held here names {name} as an application. Three things could be true and they are different: nothing has ever delegated through or to it; something did and the acts have been DROPPED, because this store keeps at most {max} and discards the oldest; or the name is spelled differently from the way a protocol presented it. The list below is every application some act actually named, which settles the third.
appChoose: Choose an application to see everything that has been delegated through it or to it. A delegation has three parties and an application can be two of them — the INTERMEDIARY that acts on somebody's behalf, and the TARGET the credential is for — so this page shows both sides of one application rather than making you pick a side. That is the question worth asking before turning a middle tier off: not what reaches it, but what exists because of it.
appListFromActsBefore: The list is built from the ACTS rather than from
appListFromActsAfter: , which is why an entry here can be marked not in the registry: the registry holds what this service has been asked about, and an RFC 8693 audience nobody has otherwise mentioned is a real delegation target that nothing else in this console knows the name of.
appUnregisteredTitle: No entry under ou=applications names this. The registry holds what this service has been ASKED ABOUT, and a delegation naming something nobody has otherwise mentioned is ordinary — an RFC 8693 audience is exactly that.
alsoPersonBefore: . It has also PRESENTED a credential of its own, so it is a person here as well as an application:
alsoPersonAfter: on the users page. That is the middle tier being both, which is ordinary — a service account authenticates, so the identity funnel files it under ou=users, and tickets are issued FOR it, so the registry files it under ou=applications.
spelledWays: It has been spelled {n} ways and they are one application here:
spelledWaysAfter: . Two spellings of one identity is two people, so they are collapsed on the same normalisation the picture uses — the spellings are kept so that the collapse is something you can see rather than take on trust.
hWhatItDoes: What it does in a delegation

hPartOf: The relationships it is part of
partOfNote: Every chain this application appears in, drawn together — so a middle tier shows the people it acts for on one side and what it reaches on the other, which is the shape a list of rows cannot show. The chain link beside each act at the foot of this page draws ONE of them alone.
partiesDealsNote: Every box in the picture above, including this application itself.
hEveryDelegated: Every delegated credential related to it

hGroupings: The groupings: which applications are joined to each other
groupDefinition: A GROUP IS A SET OF APPLICATIONS THAT CAN BE REACHED FROM ONE ANOTHER BY FOLLOWING GRANTS, IGNORING WHICH WAY EACH ONE POINTS. That is the whole definition, and the direction is dropped ON PURPOSE. A grant is directed — a client is granted a permission a resource exposes, which is why every line above has a round end and a pointed one — but following the arrows would answer what can this client eventually reach, and a permission register has no chains in it: holding a permission on an API does not grant that API's permissions to anybody. Following a grant EITHER WAY answers the question somebody actually arrives with — which applications are in the same conversation as this one — and it is the only reading under which an API and the three front ends holding permissions on it come out as ONE group rather than as four. Every picture still draws every line with its direction on it, so what is dropped is direction as a test of MEMBERSHIP, never direction as a fact.

actsLead: Who acted on whose behalf, through what, to reach what. Three of the protocol families here can delegate and each calls it something different — Kerberos has S4U2Self, two flavours of S4U2Proxy and a forwarded ticket-granting ticket; WS-Trust has OnBehalfOf and ActAs; OAuth 2.0 Token Exchange has impersonation and delegation. This page records all eight against one model, because the question people arrive with is protocol-independent: alice never touched the back end, so why is there a ticket to it in her name, and who asked for it?
actsLayers: The three columns in the middle are the layers of the architecture, and the names are this page's own rather than any protocol's — a Kerberos front end, a WS-Trust requester and an OAuth client doing an exchange are the same position in the same picture:
actsPersonOrApp: A party can be a person, an application, or both, and the middle one routinely is both: HTTP/frontend.example.com has an entry under ou=users (it authenticates, so this service files it with the people) and an entry under ou=applications (tickets are issued FOR it). Each cell links to whichever of the two exist. An application marked not in the registry is not an error — the registry holds what this service has been ASKED ABOUT, and an RFC 8693 audience nobody has otherwise mentioned is exactly that.
actsAxis: Impersonation and delegation are the axis worth filtering on, and they are not a matter of degree. Under a delegation the credential CARRIES the chain — an act claim, a composite ActAs, S4U_DELEGATION_INFO in the PAC — so the far end can see who is really asking and can decide differently because of it. Under an impersonation nothing does, which means this page is the only place it will ever be visible: no reading of the token afterwards, at the resource server or in a log, can recover the fact that a middle tier was involved.
actsRefusals: Refusals are recorded and are most of what this page is for. A delegation that worked tells you the plumbing is connected. A delegation that was refused names the two accounts, the two attributes and which of them was missing, at the moment the KDC decided — and the text in the Authorized by / why not column is the KDC's OWN words, the same sentence the client was sent, rather than a second wording that could come to disagree with it.
sameActsDrawn: The same acts drawn as a diagram — a stick figure per person, a rectangle per application, a hexagon for this service in this trust realm, and a line per relationship: who acts for whom, and what each credential was FOR.
opensWithFilter: It opens with the filter you have set here.
filterFirst: Filter first if this list is long — the picture is drawn from everything that matches, not from one page.
pivotApplication: Or pivot on an application. A delegation has three parties and an application can be two of them — the intermediary that acts on somebody's behalf, and the target the credential is for. Search for one and click it, and see everything that has been delegated through it or to it, in either role, with every credential that came out. The search follows the filter above and the page it opens does not: it shows everything that application has ever been part of, because what exists because of this thing is not a question a half-answer is useful for. Any part of a name matches, EVERY spelling an act presented is searched, and twenty are shown at a time with the rest a click away.
pivotPerson: Or pivot on a person. Everything issued in their name, end to end: every grant and flow with the exact one labelled, every assertion, ticket and SVID, the applications holding all of it, and the sign-ins it rests on — with any delegation naming them drawn in the same picture. The list includes people nothing was ever issued to, because an S4U2Self or an OnBehalfOf names somebody who was never present, and that is the row worth opening. Search it the same way — any part of a name, every spelling they arrived under, twenty at a time — and clicking a result IS the choice.
textSearchesEvery: The text box searches every party of the chain and both explanations at once, because the fact somebody arrives with names one of them and they do not know which column it will be in.
chainLinkNote: The chain link under each row's number draws THAT RELATIONSHIP on its own — the whole chain the act belongs to, with everything else in the service left out. It goes to the chain rather than to the act because an act has no picture of its own: a diagram has the times taken out, and four acts a second apart between the same three parties are one line.
nothingDelegatedYet: Nothing has delegated anything yet. Three things put a row here: a Kerberos S4U2Self, S4U2Proxy or forwarded-TGT request at the KDC; a WS-Trust RequestSecurityToken carrying <wst:OnBehalfOf> or <wst14:ActAs>; and an RFC 8693 token exchange at /oauth2/token. A REFUSED attempt counts — the delegation page in the debugger will produce one on purpose.

The last column draws one row alone, which is the answer to what is this one, exactly on a service that has been driven for an afternoon and whose whole picture is forty boxes.
hKerberosPolicy: Who may delegate to whom — Kerberos
kdcView: The KDC's view of the ONE delegation policy (#186). Kerberos, WS-Trust and the RFC 8693 token exchange are decided by the same issuance policy from the same controls on the directory's entries — the section below lists them for every protocol; this one lists the Kerberos services, whose entries are named SPN@REALM. The KDC refuses in BOTH modes, as it always has (in development the fixture services' rules are seeded onto their entries so every refusal can be reached); WS-Trust and the token exchange are enforced in product mode and, in development, recorded as what would have been refused. Every row says what allowed it, in the same column for all three families.
twoAttributes: The relationship rests on two attributes on two OPPOSITE entries — appAllowedToDelegateTo on the front end, appAllowedToActOnBehalfOf on the back end — which is why they are in one table with a column saying which entry carries the permission. Same messages, same KDC options, opposite direction of trust — and the second one turns I can write to this computer object into I can reach this service as anybody.
beyondAttribute: Each mechanism needs one thing BEYOND the attribute, and it is the same thing on every row of that kind, so it is here rather than in a column: classic needs a FORWARDABLE evidence ticket, which S4U2Self returns only where the policy allows the impersonation — impersonation in the service's appDelegationSemantics (Active Directory's TRUSTED_TO_AUTHENTICATE_FOR_DELEGATION) and a user who is not protected; resource-based needs PA-PAC-OPTIONS (padata type 167) carrying the resource-based bit, and [MS-SFU] requires a KDC to answer KDC_ERR_BADOPTION without it — an error that says nothing about padata. Resource-based needs no forwardable evidence and no flag on the front end at all, which is why it is the easier path.
noConstrainedPrincipal: No principal here is configured for constrained delegation of either kind.
accountFlagsNote: Two of these three STOP delegation rather than permit it, and the third is not a control at all. An account appears here whether or not any pair above names it, because an account named in no pair is precisely the one somebody is wondering about.
noFlags: No principal here carries one of these flags.
mechanismsNote: Read off the same table this page records against, so a mechanism cannot be recordable and undocumented, nor described here and never occur.
serviceDecides: This service decides who may do it.
nothingChecksWho: Nothing here checks who may do it.
inMemory: It is in memory and dies with the process, like the counters, the audit log, the sessions and the signing key. It also has no clear button and no way to add a row by hand, which is a decision rather than an omission: every row here is something that actually happened, and a table mixing those with typed-in ones would be worth much less than either. Restarting the service is how you get an empty one.

succeededMiddle: as an ordinary authentication row, and on

nothingChangesBefore: Nothing on this page changes anything (2026-10-01). The register's controls and delegation.maxRecords are on
nothingChangesAfter: , and one application's permissions on its own Permissions tab.
everyTablePaged: Every table on this page is paged, at {per} rows, and they share one size. There are seven of them here with several screens of prose between, so fifty rows apiece — which is what every other page in this console uses — would put the last heading tens of thousands of pixels down. ?per= changes all seven together (at most {max} rows a page) and the control above the acts table is the one that sets it. Each table then has a page parameter of ITS OWN, so moving one leaves the other six where you left them: ?page= for the acts, and ?chainsPage=, ?permissionsPage=, ?grantsPage=, ?pairsPage=, ?flagsPage= and ?mechanismsPage= for the rest. The two searches over the configured register are ?permq= and ?grantq=, and a new search starts that table at its first page.
jsonWhole: ?format=json carries the WHOLE of every list and not the page you are looking at, and that is deliberate rather than an oversight. The acts are the exception and always were: they are capped at delegation.maxRecords and can be thousands, so the reply pages them and carries page, pages and matched for a caller to walk them with. Everything else — chains, the configured policy and the whole of allowed — comes back entire, because each is derived from something already bounded and because GET /admin-api/permissions answers with that same register under its own name. A caller that had to walk seven pagings to read a register a page draws in one screen would be paying for this page's layout. allowed.filter and allowed.paging report what the BROWSER was shown, so nothing here is silent about the difference. The acts are also at GET /admin-api/delegation with the same parameters.
